skills.name: Describe the occurrence of sulphur and its extraction by the Frasch process

note.text:
Sulphur occurs free in underground beds, often near volcanoes and oil fields, and combined as sulphides (galena PbS, zinc blende ZnS, iron pyrites FeS2) and sulphates (gypsum CaSO4, barytes BaSO4).
The Frasch process brings up free sulphur from deep beds using three concentric pipes:
• Outer pipe: superheated water at about 170 °C, kept liquid under pressure, melts the sulphur (melting point about 115 °C).
• Inner pipe: hot compressed air froths the molten sulphur.
• Middle pipe: the froth, being less dense, is forced up to the surface.
The rock and sand stay underground, so the sulphur comes up about 99 per cent pure. It is run into tanks and allowed to solidify.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to say where sulphur is found and describe each stage of the Frasch process and why it gives pure sulphur.
Builds on: Form Three elements, mixtures and the idea of melting point.
Leads to: Lesson {2} (the properties of sulphur) and the compounds made from it in the rest of the chapter.

sections.heading: Where sulphur is found
sections.text:
Sulphur is found free (uncombined) in beds a few hundred metres underground, often near volcanoes and oil fields, notably in the United States, Mexico and Poland.
It is also found combined:
• as sulphides: galena {formula('PbS')}, zinc blende {formula('ZnS')}, iron pyrites {formula('FeS2')};
• as sulphates: gypsum {formula('CaSO4')}, barytes {formula('BaSO4')}.
Sulphur is also present in coal and crude oil, and in the proteins of living things.

sections.heading: The Frasch process
sections.text:
Free sulphur deep underground is brought up by the Frasch pump, which has three concentric pipes.
• Superheated water at about {170} °C is forced down the OUTER pipe. Pressure keeps it liquid above its normal boiling point, and it melts the sulphur, whose melting point is about {115} °C.
• Hot compressed air is forced down the INNER pipe. It froths the molten sulphur.
• The froth is less dense than water, so the pressure pushes it up the MIDDLE pipe to the surface, where it runs into tanks and solidifies.
Because only the sulphur melts, the rock and sand stay underground and the sulphur comes up about {99} per cent pure.

key_words.meaning: an element not joined to any other, as sulphur is in its beds
water kept liquid above {100} °C by pressure
the method of mining underground sulphur with three concentric pipes
a light mixture of gas bubbles and liquid

mistake.wrong: the compressed air burns the sulphur so it can rise
mistake.right: the air froths the molten sulphur so it is light enough to be pushed up
mistake.why: Burning would destroy the sulphur. The air only makes a light froth.

worked_example.problem: Explain why the water sent down the Frasch pump is at {t} °C and not at {100} °C.
steps: Water at {100} °C is not hot enough to melt it.
Water is kept liquid above {100} °C by the pressure in the pipe, so it can be superheated to {t} °C.
At {t} °C the water is well above {mp} °C and melts the sulphur underground.
worked_example.answer: because {mp} °C is needed to melt sulphur, which is above the normal boiling point of water

cards.idea: Sulphur occurs free underground and combined in sulphides and sulphates.
example: free in beds near oil fields; combined as {formula('PbS')}, {formula('ZnS')} and {formula('CaSO4')}

cards.idea: The Frasch pump has three concentric pipes: superheated water in, compressed air in, froth out.
example: water about {170} °C down the outer pipe; air down the inner; froth up the middle

cards.idea: Only the sulphur melts, so it comes up almost pure.
example: the rock and sand are left underground

pick.q: Why does the Frasch process give sulphur that needs no further purification?
pick.r: Only the sulphur melts at that temperature, so the rock and sand are left behind underground
w: The sulphur is distilled as it rises
Acid is added to dissolve the impurities
The water washes all the impurities away
e: No distillation takes place; the separation happens by melting.
No acid is used in the Frasch process.
Sulphur is insoluble in water, and the impurities are not washed out by it.
pick.y: Sulphur melts at about {115} °C but rock and sand do not, so only the sulphur is carried up.

pick.q: Why is the Frasch process used instead of digging the sulphur out?
pick.r: The beds lie under layers of loose, water-bearing rock that would collapse into a mine
w: Sulphur is too valuable to dig
Digging would set the sulphur on fire
The sulphur lies only a few metres down
e: Value is not the reason; the ground above the beds is.
Sulphur does not catch fire by itself when dug.
The beds lie a few HUNDRED metres down.
pick.y: Pumping melted sulphur up through pipes avoids sinking a shaft through unsafe ground.

pick.q: What happens to the molten sulphur when it reaches the surface?
pick.r: It runs into large tanks and solidifies as it cools
w: It is burned at once to sulphur dioxide
It is dissolved in water for transport
It is distilled to separate the allotropes
e: Burning it would destroy the product; some is burned later, at the factory.
Sulphur is insoluble in water.
Allotropes are not separated by distillation; they are forms of the same element.
pick.y: The froth is run into tanks, where the sulphur cools and sets as a solid ready for use.

pick.q: Roughly how pure is the sulphur brought up by the Frasch process?
w: About {50} per cent pure
About {75} per cent pure
Less than {10} per cent pure
e: Half of the mass would be impurity, which melting underground avoids.
The purity is much higher than that.
That would be an ore, not the free element.
pick.y: Because only the sulphur melts, almost nothing else comes up with it.

pick.q: Where is sulphur found as the free element?
pick.r: In underground deposits, often near volcanoes and oil fields
w: Only combined in sea water
Only in the air
Only in living plants
e: Sea water holds sulphates, which are combined sulphur, not the free element.
Air holds only traces of sulphur compounds, not the free element.
Plants hold sulphur in proteins, which is combined sulphur.
pick.y: Free sulphur occurs in beds a few hundred metres down, and combined as sulphides and sulphates.

pick.q: How many concentric pipes are used in the Frasch process?
w: One
Two
Five
e: One pipe could not carry water down and sulphur up at the same time.
A third pipe is needed for the compressed air that lifts the froth.
Three are enough: water in, air in, froth out.
pick.y: Superheated water goes down the outer pipe, hot compressed air down the inner one, and the froth rises up the middle one.

pick.q: What is sent down the outer pipe in the Frasch process, and why?
pick.r: Superheated water at about {170} °C, to melt the sulphur underground
w: Cold water, to cool the rock
Hot compressed air, to blow the sulphur up
Molten sulphur, to start the process
e: Cold water would not melt sulphur, which melts at about {115} °C.
The compressed air goes down the INNER pipe; the water goes down the outer one.
The sulphur is already in the ground; the water melts it there.
pick.y: Sulphur melts at about {115} °C, so water above that temperature, kept liquid by pressure, melts it in place.

pick.q: Why is hot compressed air forced down the inner pipe?
pick.r: It froths the molten sulphur so that the lighter froth is pushed up the middle pipe
w: It burns the sulphur to sulphur dioxide
It cools the molten sulphur so it sets
It dissolves the sulphur in water
e: Burning would destroy the product; the air is there to lift it.
Hot air does not set the sulphur; the froth must stay molten to rise.
Sulphur is insoluble in water.
pick.y: The froth of air and molten sulphur is less dense, so the pressure pushes it up the middle pipe.

pick.q: Why is sulphur from the Frasch process very pure?
pick.r: Only the sulphur melts and is pushed up; the rock and sand stay behind
w: It is purified later by distillation
It is washed with acid at the surface
It is crystallised from water
e: No further purification is needed; it comes up about {99} per cent pure.
No acid washing is used in the process.
Sulphur is insoluble in water, so it cannot be crystallised from it.
pick.y: Melting separates the sulphur from the rock underground, so it arrives almost pure.

pick.q: the superheated water down to the sulphur bed
pick.y: Water goes down the outer pipe, air down the inner pipe, and the froth comes up the middle one.
The innermost pipe carries air, which froths the molten sulphur so it can rise.

pick.q: the froth of molten sulphur to the surface
pick.w3: The same pipe as the water
pick.y: The froth rises between the water pipe and the air pipe, that is up the middle one.

pick.q: Put the stages of the Frasch process in order.
s: Three concentric pipes are sunk down to the sulphur bed
Superheated water at about {170} °C is forced down the outer pipe
The sulphur in the bed melts
Hot compressed air is forced down the inner pipe and froths the molten sulphur
The froth is pushed up the middle pipe and runs into tanks to solidify

pick.q: Put these stages of getting sulphur from the ground in order, starting with the deepest.
s: Solid sulphur lies in a bed a few hundred metres down
Heat from the superheated water reaches the bed
The sulphur melts and collects at the foot of the pipes
Air bubbles make the molten sulphur into a light froth
The froth reaches the surface and is run off

pick.q: Put these stages of testing a sample from a Frasch well in order.
s: A sample of the solid from the tank is taken
Its colour is noted: a brittle yellow solid
A little is shaken with water and does not dissolve
A little is shaken with carbon disulphide and dissolves
A little is heated in air and burns with a blue flame
